This guy came across as surprisingly creepy to me, though I'm not sure if that was intended by the author. It's his total indifference to the deaths of his servants, not only the deaths themselves but his having personally ordered them to die in one way or another. Even if he is attempting to limit the number of people he's exposed to, he's still totally okay with having basically enslaved a number of them. It's like he went so far from sociopathy it looped around and approached it from the other end.

And on top of that he's tall, gaunt and finds everything enjoyable, presumably including criminal acts. He's about two steps removed from being The Joker as an SCP.

item.title: Re: Decimal places, precision, and variability.
item.content:encoded: That assumes that 230 was weighed once and only once, and/or that the (in-universe) report has not been updated with new info since it was originally written. Neither scenario makes sense to me. More realistically, 230 (and most other living SCPs) would regularly have their vitals taken (daily or weekly), including height and weight, with the article updated as more data is collected and analyzed. In this case, a mass of "68.04 kg" would mean that the majority of times 230 was weighed, he weighed between 68.035 and 68.045 kg (conveniently, between 149.99 and 150.01 lb).

item.title: Re: Decimal places, precision, and variability.
item.content:encoded: Measurement's to two points on this one because it's not meant to represent fluctuating weight, just the exact weight of the item at the time that the article is supposed to have been written.

item.title: Decimal places, precision, and variability.
item.content:encoded:
Huh. I didn’t expect to need this thing so soon, but listing 230’s mass to two decimal places is too silly to ignore.

[soapbox]

Adding decimal places to a measurement not only implies a certain level of precision, but also a level of variability in the value of the measurement. Specifically, listing the mass of something to the nearest 0.01 kg implies that its mass usually does not fluctuate more than 0.005 kg (5 g, or the mass of a US nickel) above or below the listed value. While I have no doubt that one could get the mass of a person accurate to a fraction of a gram at any given moment, I have a much harder time believing that the mass of any creature with an active metabolism does not significantly fluctuate over the course of a day, week, or year. Heck, a normal person can very quickly (like, in minutes) lose five grams just by sweating - and 230 literally oozes charm ecstasy.

If this were an inanimate object, something with a constant mass, then I’d have no problem if its mass were listed to two or even more decimal places. But the only way such precision would work for the mass of a living thing would be if its mass didn’t change, which (I would think) would be noted somewhere in the article.

I’m just looking for appropriate precision – not every measurement needs to go to three decimal places, and many don’t need any. And a measurement with more decimal places than expected precision would warrant looks… well, silly.

Thank you.

[/soapbox]

Also, 150 lb doesn’t seem especially gaunt even for a guy who’s 6-1, but that’s a whole ‘nother debate.

item.content:encoded:
I was preparing to rage at this until I actually read it.

My main criticism is that there's very little that isn't explained. The whole point of the SCPs is that we are terrified of the effect and know next to nothing of the cause. For example, the Sculpture, the very first SCP. I would suggest that as a template for any and all SCPs. While I may be remiss in a few of my own works, I think I did a very fine job with SCP-139 if I say so myself. If you notice in that one, the artifact is never actually even observably the cause of any incident. It's SCPs like this that are truly effective.

I would try to make this far more obtuse and oblique, therefore inciting more emotion and less intellectual stimulation.
